10382-memoir-of-william-watts-mcnair-lat:
J. E. Howard wrote this memoir of William Watts McNair, first European explorer of Kafiristan, for the Royal Geographical Society. McNair, born in 1849, joined the Indian Survey Department at eighteen in 1867 and served faithfully until his death from fever at Mussooree in 1889. Howard praises rare, modest worth too little known.

The memoir traces McNair's twelve years with the Rajputana party, his Mysore service, and his daring journey into Kafiristan, a land then closed to Europeans. Survey notes and official praise back the tale. Readers get a respectful portrait of a quiet surveyor-explorer in Victorian India.
12736-masters-of-the-english-novel-a-stu:
Richard Burton's Masters of the English Novel, a study of principles and personalities, opens by noting that all the world loves a story as it loves a lover. Fiction, a broad term for story-telling, is hoary, told since man walked erect and long before records. Burton regards it in various ways, as art, as history and as moral force.

Chapters move from Richardson and Fielding through Smollett, Sterne, Austen, Scott, French influence, Dickens, Thackeray, George Eliot, Trollope, Hardy, Meredith, Stevenson and the American contribution. Burton writes as a teacher-critic, clear and enthusiastic. The book offers a readable survey of the English novel's growth, from beginnings to modern masters.
15364-the-pronunciation-of-english-words:
John Sargeaunt wrote this tract for the Society for Pure English, printed at the Clarendon Press in 1920, with a preface and notes by Henry Bradley. It asks how English speakers should say words taken from Latin, a question that touches everyday speech, school teaching, and the reading of older books. Notes and letters from other scholars follow the main paper.

The tract starts with history: Latin reached England as a living tongue with Pope Gregory's missionaries in the seventh century, and its sound changed over time. Sargeaunt then sets out rules for stress and vowel sound in Latin-derived words, with examples. For readers who care about clear speech, it offers a reasoned standard rather than fashion or guesswork, grounded in how Latin was once spoken in England.
16912-the-life-of-the-right-honourable-h:
Mr. Harrison wrote this life of Horatio, Lord Viscount Nelson, in two volumes, volume one printed at the Ranelagh Press in London. The title page lists Nelson's honors at length: Baron of the Nile, knight of the Bath, duke of Bronte, vice-admiral of the White, and more. A king's answer on Trafalgar praises Nelson's heroic services as a lasting source of strength to his dominions.

Harrison opens Nelson's life in the admiring style of his age, from youth and early service toward the fame that would crown him. The volume gives a full, early life of Britain's great sea hero, in two parts. Readers of naval history will find a rich, period portrait, useful for its detail and its view of how Nelson was first remembered.
16913-the-life-of-the-right-honourable-h:
Mr. Harrison wrote this life of Horatio, Lord Viscount Nelson, in two volumes, volume two printed at the Ranelagh Press in London. The title page lists Nelson's honors at length: Baron of the Nile, knight of the Bath, duke of Bronte, vice-admiral of the White, and more. A king's answer on Trafalgar praises Nelson's heroic services as a lasting source of strength to his dominions.

Harrison tells Nelson's life in the admiring style of his age, with battles, honors, and death at Trafalgar at its heart. The volume gives a full, early life of Britain's great sea hero. Readers of naval history will find a rich, period portrait, useful for its detail and its view of how Nelson was first remembered.
19533-stories-of-great-inventors-fulton-:
This children's book tells the stories of great inventors: Fulton, Whitney, Morse, Cooper, Edison, and others, in short sentences set as separate paragraphs. Each life is told through work and patience, not birth or luck.

One scene shows young Finley taking a drawing to Mr. West, hearing it is not finished, and returning home to work again after his faults are pointed out. The book's lesson is plain: invention grows from steady practice and honest correction. Each life stresses work and patience over luck or birth. Whitney's section follows his government firearms contract at Whitneyville, where a waterfall drove his machines.
21251-the-jefferson-lemen-compact-the-re:
Willard C. MacNaul read this paper before the Chicago Historical Society in February 1915. He argued that Thomas Jefferson and James Lemen worked together to keep slavery out of Illinois and the Northwest Territory. Related documents from 1781 to 1818 support the claim. The University of Chicago Press published it the same year.

MacNaul traces slavery in Illinois under Governors St. Clair and Harrison, the Ordinance of 1787 that barred it, and Lemen's anti-slavery work in the Baptist churches. He found his materials while preparing a history of Illinois Baptists. Later historians have debated the compact story, which makes the paper itself part of the argument.
21635-prudence-says-so:
Ethel Hueston's Prudence Says So, copyrighted in 1916, returns to the parsonage family of Prudence of the Parsonage. Prudence dresses down her sister Connie for putting shoes on too soon and wrinkling her dress. The Ladies' Aid gave Connie the dainty dress for her birthday.

Chapters treat a chaperon, a spoiled wedding, a serenade, and a case of substitution. Carol, Lark, Fairy, and the twins fill the house with schemes and scrapes. Arthur William Brown draws the pictures for Grosset and Dunlap's edition. Hueston dedicated the warm, funny tale to her small daughter Elizabeth.
23359-quite-so:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich drew this Civil War camp tale from the Army of the Potomac after the first battle of Bull Run. The men, shattered and downcast, lie behind earthworks while ambulances creep toward Washington and the field at Manassas still holds its dead.

Among them is a soldier nicknamed Quite So, whose true name is John Bladburn, a man the camp knows by a catch phrase that stuck like a burr. Aldrich follows him through camp talk, marches, and quiet acts of nerve, sketching war as soldiers felt it rather than as generals planned it. The tale honours a plain man's grit, and the odd, fond names that comrades give each other in hard times.
23488-the-jacobite-rebellions-1689-1746-:
J. Pringle Thomson edited this Bell's Scottish History source book on the Jacobite rebellions from sixteen eighty nine to seventeen forty six, a companion to a volume on the Scottish Covenanters. Rather than a single narrative, it gathers sources: letters, proclamations, reports, and memoirs from the years of rising and defeat.

Students meet the Stuart cause, the Highland hosts, and the Hanoverian response in the words of those who lived them, with editorial notes to guide reading. The book suits school and college study, where first hand voices matter more than summary. Readers of Scottish history will gain a direct sense of why men rose for a lost king, and what those risings cost both sides.
24633-early-double-monasteries-a-paper-r:
Constance Stoney of Newnham College, Cambridge, read this paper before the Heretics' Society on 6 December 1914, and it was published at Cambridge and London in 1915. Its subject is the double monastery, a house for both men and women, as old as Christian monasticism itself.

Stoney notes that the phrase monasteria duplicia dates from about the sixth century, and that Bede uses the term for twin houses such as Wearmouth and Jarrow. Her paper traces how double houses worked, who ruled them, and why they faded. Readers of church history will find it a short, learned, and clear study.
27747-personal-recollections-from-early-:
Martha Somerville edited these personal recollections of her mother, Mary Somerville, the Scottish science writer, with selections from her correspondence. The fifth thousand was published in London by John Murray in 1874.

Chapters follow Mary from childhood in Scotland through Edinburgh society, two marriages, and a career that produced The Mechanism of the Heavens and Physical Geography. Letters from Herschel, Whewell, and Brougham show a woman who taught herself mathematics and astronomy and won a place among Europe's leading scientists. Contents also cover Edinburgh supper parties, a tour in the Highlands, the mutiny in the fleet, and the battle of Camperdown.
30482-the-international-spy-being-the-se:
Allen Upward, writing as Monsieur A. V., presents The International Spy as the secret history of the Russo-Japanese War, copyrighted in 1904 and 1905. Contents open with a prologue on the two empresses. They follow the instructions of Monsieur V, the hint of Princess Y, the head of the Manchurian syndicate, and the Czar's autograph.

Later chapters stage a dinner with the enemy, drugging and kidnapping, and a race for Siberia. They add the Czar's message, the betrothal of Delilah, the answer of the Mikado, and the secret service of Japan. Upward blends espionage romance with war politics, letting spies, princes, and syndicates move the plot. The novel reads as a brisk, conspiratorial thriller of empires at war.
31691-the-bacillus-of-long-life-a-manual:
Loudon M. Douglas's manual on the bacillus of long life and the prolonging of human existence opens with a history of milk, one of the oldest foods known to mankind. It notes cattle among nomadic peoples in Paleolithic and Neolithic times, butter making in India 1500 years before Christ, and the milks of camels, buffaloes, sheep, and goats used across the East.

From that history the book turns to preparation and use: how fermented milk foods are made and why their bacillus was thought to lengthen life. Readers get an early twentieth-century health manual, part history and part practical instruction, from a period fascinated by diet and longevity.
31999-the-natural-philosophy-of-william-:
W. James King, curator of electricity at the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology, wrote this paper on William Gilbert and the thinkers who came before him. Gilbert was an English physician whose book on the loadstone, De magnete, appeared in 1600. It has long been credited with laying a base for the modern science of electricity and magnetism. King tests that credit by setting Gilbert's account of the loadstone beside explanations found in the Middle Ages and earlier.

His verdict revises the usual praise: Gilbert is best understood not as a herald of a wholly new science, but as a modifier of older ideas. The paper also weighs what Gilbert truly added. It also asks in what sense he depended on earlier writers, so readers can judge his place in the history of science with more care.
32982-student-s-hand-book-of-mushrooms-o:
Thomas Taylor's Student's Hand-Book of Mushrooms of America, Edible and Poisonous, teaches readers to know American mushrooms by picture and description. It was published in Washington in 1897 in serial numbers at fifty cents each. Plate A presents the common field mushroom, Agaricus campester. Its figures show the mature plant, a sectional view, the basidia and sterigmata that bear spores, the mycelium, and spores as shed and magnified. Later plates show types of the six orders of hymenomycetes.

Taylor, author of works on food products, writes for students who needed to tell safe mushrooms from dangerous ones. That skill was practical in a country where wild fungi were gathered for the table. His plates, drawn by himself, give the book its lasting value, combining science with careful art. For mycologists and historians of natural history, it is a clear early American guide to a field that rewards caution.
603-letters-of-george-borrow-to-the-brit:
George Borrow writes to the British and Foreign Bible Society in these letters, edited by T. H. Darlow and published in 1911. From Norwich in 1833 onward, Borrow reports on Manchu, Tartar tongues, and gospel versions, arguing over translations with sharp, learned candor. His letters show a linguist at work for a missionary cause.

Borrow writes with energy and pride, claiming he can translate Manchu with Amyot's aid and judge a Matthew version fairly. The letters track his road from scholar to agent in Spain and Russia. The volume serves as a vivid record of a restless mind, where language study and faith share the same road.
615-orlando-furioso:
Ludovico Ariosto continues Boiardo's unfinished Orlando romance in this vast Renaissance epic, here in William Stewart Rose's translation. Orlando, Rinaldo, Angelica, and the peers of Charlemagne chase love and war across France, Africa, and Cathay. Magic waters, sieges, and duels fill the interwoven tales.

Ariosto writes with wit, grace, and irony, letting heroes grow mad, sane, and foolish by turns. An introduction sums Boiardo's plot for new readers, so none need start lost. The poem endures as a masterpiece of chivalric fantasy, where love drives knights madder than any sword.
britannica-1911-albinoni-tomasso:
Albinoni, Tomasso, an Italian musician who lived from about 1674 to about 1745, receives a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Venice. As a composer he was prolific, writing operas in great number. Those operas drew the attention of his contemporaries for their originality, the entry records.

Posterity, though, kept a different part of his output in view. Albinoni is more remarkable, the entry judges, as a composer of instrumental music. That music greatly attracted Bach, the strongest witness the short notice could call. Bach wrote at least two fugues on themes by Albinoni. He also used Albinoni's bass lines constantly as harmony exercises for his own pupils. Few composers of operas can claim a second life of that kind, supplying study material in the workshop of a greater master.
britannica-1911-borelli-giovanni-alfonso:
Giovanni Alfonso Borelli (1608–1679) was an Italian thinker who explained the body's motions by the laws of machines. Born at Naples, he became professor of mathematics at Messina in 1649 and at Pisa in 1656. In 1667 he went back to Messina, but in 1674 he was forced to Rome, where Queen Christina of Sweden sheltered him until his death.

His best-known work, De motu animalium (1680–1681), treats animal movement on mechanical principles, and the entry ranks him as founder of the iatrophysical school. In a 1665 letter under a false name he first proposed that a comet moves in a parabola. Another book weighed attraction's pull on Jupiter's moons. Restored editions of Euclid and Apollonius and works on fevers, kidneys, and earthquakes fill out the long list.
britannica-1911-cherso:
Cherso is an island in the Adriatic Sea, off the east coast of Istria, from which the channel of Farasina divides it. Its people numbered 8,274 in 1900, and it lies in the Gulf of Quarnero. A turn bridge over the channel of Ossero joins it to Lussin, and the Canale di Mezzo lies toward Veglia. With those islands it forms the district of Lussin in Austrian Istria.

The island runs about 40 miles long and from one and a quarter to seven miles wide, with an area of 150 square miles. A mountain range crosses it, rising to 2,090 feet at the peak of Syss, and terraces hold vines and olive trees. Springs are scarce, so houses keep cisterns for rain water. Lake Vrana, deep and set near the centre, likely draws on underground sources.
britannica-1911-kelso:
Kelso is a police burgh and market town of Roxburghshire, Scotland, on the left bank of the Tweed, 52 miles southeast of Edinburgh. Its people numbered 4008 in 1901. The name is held to come from the Old Welsh calch, or Anglo Saxon cealc, chalk, with the Scots how, a hollow. The older forms Calkon and Calchon show the root more clearly.

The ruined abbey, dedicated to the Virgin and St John the Evangelist, was founded in 1128 by David I. He settled it with monks from Tiron in Picardy, moved there from Selkirk, where they had been placed fifteen years before. The building was finished toward the middle of the 13th century and grew into one of the great abbeys of the border country. The entry gives the town the usual gazetteer care: its site on the Tweed, its abbey, its markets, and its place in border history.
britannica-1911-kousso:
Kousso, also written Kosso or Cusso, is a drug made from the flower heads of Brayera anthelmintica, a handsome tree of the rose family. The tree grows 60 feet high across the table-land of Abyssinia, at heights of 3000 to 8000 feet above the sea. The drug is shipped as tight rolls, about 18 inches long and 2 inches thick, formed of the whole flower head bound round with a band. Its active part is a substance called koussin or kosin.

Kousso is taken as a dose of the powder, or as a rough infusion of the coarsely ground flowers, swallowed with the liquid. It is held to be a sure cure for the tapeworm Taenia solium. In action it stands close to male fern, but it is much weaker than that drug. For that reason it is very rarely used in Great Britain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adso:
Adso, Abbot of Moutier-en-Der's Cluniac monastery, died in 992 on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and ranks among the tenth century's foremost writers. Rich, noble parents raised him; he was educated at Luxeuil Abbey, called to Toul to instruct the clergy, becoming Moutier-en-Der's abbot in 960. His friends included Gerbert, later Silvester II, and Abbo of Fleury, with other famous men of his time.

Hymns and saints' lives fill his writings, among them St. Mansuetus of Toul's life and a verse rendering of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, book two, and a tractate De Antichristo in letter form to Queen Gerberga, wife of Louis IV. Rabanus Maurus, Alcuin, and even St. Augustine have all been credited with that last work, and Dollinger quotes it among medieval writings on Antichrist. His works appear in Migne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-angelo-car:
Blessed Angelo Carletti of Chivasso, a Franciscan moral theologian, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Chivasso in Piedmont in 1411, he died at Coni in 1495. Holy from youth, he took a doctorate in civil and canon law at Bologna and entered the Friars Minor about the age of thirty.

Four times his brothers chose him vicar-general of the Cismontane Observance, the Italian branch of the order. His Summa Angelica, a handbook of cases of conscience, became a standard confessor's guide. The entry presents a lawyer-friar whose book served priests for generations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-henry-suso:
Blessed Henry Suso, a German Dominican mystic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Constance about 1295, taking his mother's family name of Süs, he died at Ulm in 1366. He entered the Dominicans at thirteen, studied at Constance and Cologne, and sat at the feet of Meister Eckhart's school.

His influence ran strongest in women's convents, above all Katherinenthal and Töss, where Elsbeth Stagel preserved his letters and drew from him his life story. As a preacher he reached towns across Swabia, Switzerland, Alsace, and the Low Countries, working person by person rather than with crowds. His Little Book of Eternal Wisdom remains his best-known work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boso:
Boso, first Bishop of Merseburg and Apostle of the Wends, won a hostile people by preaching in their own tongue. A Benedictine of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, he was called to Otto I's court, since converting the newly subdued Wends seemed vital to German security. At first his mission failed, as the Wends hated the Germans who had taken their freedom.

He studied the Wendish language, worked for their material and spiritual good without self-interest, and turned hatred to love. In 968 he helped create three sees, Merseburg, Meissen, and Zeitz, choosing Merseburg for himself. Hugo took Zeitz and Burchard took Meissen, all three consecrated on Christmas Day 968 by Adalbert of Magdeburg. Boso died on a visit to Bavaria in November 970.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-mus:
Thomas Plassmann's entry treats Cornelius Musso, Friar Minor Conventual and Bishop of Bitonto, prominent at the Council of Trent. Born at Piacenza in 1511, he died in 1574. Perhaps his day's most renowned orator, he was justly styled the Italian Demosthenes. Returning to ancient patristic models, he raised the homily to its highest perfection. Among the first three bishops present at Trent, he delivered the inaugural oration, distinguishing himself especially in the Justification debates.

In 1560 he was sent as papal legate to Emperor Ferdinand. His works include De divina historia libri tres, Venice, 1585 and 1587; Commentarius in epistolam ad Romanos, Venice, 1588; and De operibus sex dierum, Venice, 1598. His Conciones evangeliorum and Sermones, edited by Jos. Musso at Venice in 1580, were translated into Latin by Michael of Isselt at Cologne in 1594. Musso was buried in Rome's Church of the Twelve Apostles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-ximenez:
Diego Ximenez de Enciso was a Spanish dramatic poet born in Andalusia about 1585. All trace of him ends after 1632, and the date of his death is unknown. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes the praise he won from Cervantes, Lope de Vega, and Montalvan. The last called him a model for writers of great comedies, yet his plays have largely sunk into oblivion.

Barrera lists eleven plays by Enciso, most of them scattered through the libraries of Europe. Only three reached several editions, among them The Medici of Florence, the one most open to modern readers. His work is marked by lofty tone, simple and gripping plots, and sonorous verse, with the eleven-syllable line ruling his versification.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-federigo-freg:
Federigo Fregoso was a Genoese cardinal, soldier, humanist, and scholar. Born about 1480, he received the archbishopric of Salerno from Julius II in 1507. As his brother's counsellor he led Genoa's army and fleet. He beat the corsair Cortogoli and raided the island of Djerba, returning with great booty.

Exiled in 1522 after Charles V took Genoa, he fled to safety aboard a French vessel. Francis I gave him the rich abbey of St Benignus at Dijon. Named cardinal in 1539, he died at Gubbio in 1541. His grieving people called him the father of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ant:
Francesco Antonio Begnudelli-Basso was a canonist, an expert in church law, who lived late in the seventeenth century and died at Freising on 9 October 1713. A native of Trent, he served as vicar-general there from 1675. He then held a canonry at Freising cathedral from 1679 and became vicar-general of that diocese in 1696, the office he held at his death.

His reputation rests on one large work, the Bibliotheca juris canonico-civilis practica. It is a repertory of the more practical questions in both church and civil courts, published at Freising in 1712 and reprinted at Geneva, Modena, and Venice. It ranked him with the best canonists of his day, praised for keen legal judgment and for speaking in the clearest terms of papal infallibility. Later editions of Ferraris's Bibliotheca surpassed it and ended its practical use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gravina-and-m:
Gravina and Montepeloso is a diocese in southern Italy, directly subject to the Holy See, counting nine parishes and twenty-eight thousand souls. Gravina, on a river of the same name in Bari province, has been an episcopal see since the ninth century. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a union made in 1818.

In 1818 Gravina was united aeque principaliter with Montepeloso, a twelfth-century see suffragan of Potenza. Its town defended itself against the Saracens in 975. Gravina's cathedral treasures an arm of Saint Thomas à Becket, obtained by Bishop Roberto in 1179. Notable bishops include Samuele, who built the church of the Madonna di Altamura at his own expense, and Giacomo II, who changed the rite from Greek to Latin in 1302.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luca-cambiaso:
Luca Cambiaso, also called Luchetto da Genova, was a Genoese painter, born at Moneglia in 1527 and dead at the Escorial in 1585. His father Giovanni taught him, and is credited with a method of squaring the body to get foreshortening right.

A friend's help took Luca to Florence and Rome to study Michelangelo. Early work ran extravagant, later work calmed into clear colour and graceful pose, painted fast, often with both hands at once, amid glowing colour and rich architecture. Philip II called him to Spain in 1583 for Escorial ceilings and altarpieces. Grief over his wife's death and a refused dispensation to wed her sister wore him into melancholy, and he died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-fernan:
Martin Fernandez de Enciso was a navigator and geographer, born at Seville about 1470 and dead probably about 1528 at Seville. In 1509 Alonso de Ojeda won government of Terra Firme round Darien but lacked funds, so Enciso, reputed rich, able, and adventurous, agreed to supply a ship, men, and provisions.

Ojeda sailed ahead in 1509, Enciso following in 1510 to find Ojeda beaten by Indians, spent, and back seeking him. Taking Ojeda's survivors, Enciso founded Santa Maria la Antigua del Darien in 1510. Among his men, Vasco Nunez de Balboa had stowed away to flee creditors. Soon Balboa stirred revolt, deposed Enciso, and banished him to Spain. Enciso complained to the king, who sent Pedrarias Davila as Darien governor in 1514 to right his wrongs. Back in Spain he published Suma de Geografia in 1519, the first Spanish account of New World discoveries, reprinted in 1530 and 1549 and more accurate than rival early works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-torquato-tass:
Torquato Tasso, Italian poet, was born at Sorrento in 1544 and died at Rome in 1595. Son of Bernardo Tasso, also a writer, he enriched Renaissance Italy with an epic glorifying the Crusades. His deep Catholic feeling matched Rome's growing resistance to the Reformation in the later sixteenth century.

Educated at the Urbino court, Venice and Padua, he wrote Rinaldo before twenty and had already drafted the first canto of his great poem on Godfrey de Bouillon. At Ferrara, in Cardinal Louis d'Este's suite, he finished the Gerusalemme Liberata and wrote the pastoral Aminta in 1573. After 1575 religious scruples and literary anxieties weighed on him, even as he kept consulting learned friends over the poem's final form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-treviso:
A diocese in Venetia, in northern Italy, whose capital sits ringed by the River Sile and served as a summer resort of the Venetian nobility. Its cathedral, raised in 1141, was reshaped in 1485 by Tullio and Pietro Lombardo. Modernized in 1758 with five cupolas, it holds sculptures by the Bregno brothers and paintings by Titian and others.

The city was Roman from 183 B.C., survived as a Gothic stronghold, and was spared in the Lombard invasion of 569 through Bishop Felix. Its natives include the painters Paris Bordone and the Pennacchi brothers, the historian Odorigo Rinaldi, and the poet Venantius Fortunatus.
doe-osti-2583530-performance-evaluation-:
Latimer Controls claims its software can turn a solar farm into a flexible grid resource, and NREL built the testbed to check. Report NREL/TP-5D00-93167, dated February 4, 2025, closes CRADA CRD-23-23745, with Jing Wang as the laboratory's contact. Solar is a zero-marginal-cost, zero-emission resource; with advanced controls it can also hold back headroom and respond to grid needs. Latimer's tools use machine learning and hierarchical inverter set point allocation to estimate that headroom.

Validation happened in hardware-in-the-loop: real control hardware wired into a simulated plant and grid, realistic but de-risked. Latimer reached NREL through two voucher awards from the American-Made Solar Prize Round 6. Together the teams ran the tests, analyzed the data, and drew conclusions about performance under real-world scenarios. A vendor's algorithm meeting a national laboratory's testbed is how claims become evidence.
doe-osti-3006896-a-membrane-based-approa:
Final report for DOE grant DE-SC0021260, submitted by Christine Duval of Case Western Reserve University in December 2025, closes out a five-year project on purifying medical isotopes with membranes. The work set out to replace packed chromatography columns, whose absorbed ligands can break down, with membrane adsorbers carrying ligands bound firmly to the surface.

Duval's team made the membranes by electrospinning and grafting single or polymer ligands onto them, then measured pore size, surface area, and uptake in both batch and flow-through tests. A membrane that traps the wanted isotope quickly can cut processing from hours to minutes and shrink waste volumes. Team members also tested the materials with actinium-225 at Brookhaven National Laboratory. Results went out through journal papers, conference talks, and school outreach workshops.
doe-osti-3365799-supercapacitor-based-po:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-20849, by Joseph R. Sleppy and Alisa J. Silverstein of Capacitech Energy with Ramesh Koripella and Waylon T. Clark of Sandia, demonstrates supercapacitor storage for grid resilience. Supercapacitors release and absorb power almost instantly but store little energy, suiting them to ride-through and power quality jobs. The demonstration, run with the Orlando Utilities Commission, evaluated Capacitech's C-Link module built around a 3.6-farad, 720-volt rated system.

Cell balancing gets detailed treatment, because mismatched cells overcharge unevenly. In overvoltage experiments the C-Link's active protection corrected a voltage imbalance in about two minutes. The modeled passive resistor approach needed two hours. The unit kept dissipating roughly 8 watt-hours after charging stopped to pull voltage below its rating. Enclosure strength, form factor, and temperature checks round out the record.
doe-osti-3452082-characterization-result:
ORNL/TM-2026/4647 is a June 2026 report from Oak Ridge National Laboratory that characterizes BANR TRISO fuel particles. Grant W. Helmreich, Katherine I. Montoya, and Wesley Jones wrote the results. TRISO particles carry coated fuel kernels meant to trap fission products.

Data forms record layer imaging with an optical microscope system. One mount is logged with its folder path, zoom, and calibration values. Pixel calibration reached 2.9423 pixels per micron for the run shown. Calibration expiry dates are tracked on the form. Careful layer records like these let fuel makers prove coating quality batch by batch. Data forms in the report preserve the imaging settings for each coated particle sample.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GarrisonJimPlay:
Playboy magazine sat New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison down for one of its candid interviews. Garrison laid out his Kennedy assassination investigation for a mass audience. In the course of it he named Clay Shaw and David Ferrie, the two New Orleans men at the center of his case.

The Playboy interview format let public figures talk at length and without a script. For Garrison, it was a chance to take his charges past the courtroom and the evening news. The interview preserves his case in his own voice, as millions of magazine readers first encountered it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SocietyofProfes: Members of the Society of Professional Journalists received a special report in October 1996 marking the group's 30th anniversary. It was mailed out as a single report rather than published as a book. The record preserves the text of that anniversary mailing. It shows how a national press organization chose to present its own history and work to its members at the thirty-year mark.
letters-of-george-borrow-to-the-british-:
George Borrow's letters to the British and Foreign Bible Society appeared in 1911. T. H. Darlow edited them for Hodder and Stoughton. He dedicated them to the Society's committee chairman, Williamson Lamplough.

Borrow served the Society as its agent abroad for many years. His first letter here is dated February 10, 1833, from Norwich. He answers a committee letter even on a Sunday morning, he jokes. The correspondence follows his travels selling and placing Bibles. Readers meet the author of Lavengro at work, before fame. Russia and Spain figure large in his Bible Society service. His reports home mix travel adventure with committee business.
masters-of-the-english-novel-a-study-of-:
Richard Burton wrote Masters of the English Novel as a study of rules and lives. Fourteen chapters trace the form from its start to his own day. Richardson and Fielding share the first two studies of the 1700s.

Smollett and Sterne come next, then Jane Austen under the head of realism. Scott, Dickens, Thackeray, and George Eliot each get a chapter. Burton says the novel grew into a modern voice for its age. Hardy, Meredith, Stevenson, and the American gift close his wide survey. Burton weighs the men as much as their books in each study. Form, life, and the taste of the times all count in his scale.
memoir-of-william-watts-mcnair-late-of-c:
J. E. Howard wrote the memoir of William Watts McNair of the Indian Survey. McNair lived late at Connaught House, Mussooree, as the title states. Howard gave the book to the Royal Geographical Society of London.

McNair was born on September 13, 1849, and joined the Survey in 1867. He died of fever on August 13, 1889, at Mussooree. In Afghanistan he mapped the Lughman Valley and roads toward Kafiristan. The record calls him the first European to explore that land in full. His first twelve years went to topographical work in Rajputana and Mysore. Plane table skill marked him out from his first years of service.
nasa-tm-19650010116-kelvin-helmholtz-ins:
S P Talwar wrote this October 1964 Goddard paper on a plasma problem called Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. A plasma is a hot gas made of charged particles. The instability grows where flows slide past each other, much like wind raising waves on water. Here the plasma is anisotropic, meaning its properties differ by direction.

Talwar works through the theory for that uneven case. Direction matters in a magnetized plasma, because forces act differently along and across the field. A careful model helps explain waves and mixing in space plasmas. The paper is a compact theory study, aimed at specialists.
nasa-tm-19670023226-performance-of-10-ki:
Gary C. Goldman and Kenneth Yass, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, evaluated an artificial sun in this report. The machine is a commercially available carbon-arc solar radiation simulator, rated at ten kilowatts. Space hardware must be tested under realistic sunlight before it flies.

The simulator used molded lenses to even out its light, and a tungsten electrode that is not consumed, for long runs. The team measured its brightness, uniformity, and spectrum. They also checked how parallel the beam was, how steady it stayed, and how efficient it was. Knowing a simulator's flaws keeps test results from being misread.
nasa-tm-19680027788-gamma-heating-in-thi:
John H. Lynch, Richard J. Crum, and Harry J. Reilly of Lewis Research Center calculate gamma heating in thin heavy-element absorbers for this 1968 report. Their case is a thin tungsten detector placed inside a water shield. Engineers must convert heating measured with a water-based dosimeter into heating in the tungsten.

Two effects drive the conversion. First, tungsten and water absorb gamma energy at different rates per gram. Second, a skin heating effect acts at the detector surface. One-dimensional transport calculations produced response polynomials for the heating ratio. The ratio depends on source energy, shield thickness, and detector thickness. Electron transport effects were also examined, and useful results appear as graphs.
nasa-tm-19700025129-magnetic-and-kinetic:
L. F. Burlaga and K. W. Ogilvie of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in July 1970. It treats magnetic and kinetic pressures in the solar wind. The solar wind is the steady stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun, carrying the Sun's magnetic field with it.

The pair work from Explorer 34 solar wind data gathered from June to December 1967. Over spans longer than two days, the two pressures rise and fall together, they find. Within about an hour, though, a rise in one tends to match a drop in the other. They also report that average total pressure barely changes with wind speed, so speed alone does not set it.
nasa-tm-19720008559-computer-program-for:
E B Klunker, Jerry C South Jr, and Ruby M Davis of the Langley Research Center wrote this user's manual in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2437. The program computes supersonic airflow around cones. It handles round cones, oval cones, and double oval cones. Some runs place the cone at an angle to the flow. The method of lines does the underlying mathematics.

The manual explains how to run cases with little hand work. The program starts from a known or easily found solution. It then steps through changed settings in a planned sequence. Each step reuses the last answer as its starting point. That automation saved engineers many hours of setup. Aerodynamicists used such flows to check theory and design nose shapes.
orlando-furioso:
Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, Orlando Enraged, is the great Italian romance epic of Charlemagne's knights, printed here in William Stewart Rose's English verse translation. Ariosto took up the story where Matteo Maria Boiardo's Orlando Innamorato broke off at Boiardo's death in 1494, and carried the same knights, ladies, and enchantments forward.

The editor's introduction retells the starting knot. Angelica, princess of Cathay, arrives at Charlemagne's court so beautiful that every peer burns for her; her brother Argalia must first be beaten in combat. When the heathen knight Ferrau kills Argalia, Angelica flees with Orlando and Rinaldo both in pursuit, while magic waters reverse their loves. Kings of Tartary, Circassia, and Africa crowd into the chase that drives the poem.
stories-of-great-inventors-fulton-whitne:
Hattie E. Macomber wrote Stories of Great Inventors for the Educational Publishing Company, copyrighted in 1897, as part of a young folk's library of choice literature. The title page names the five lives inside: Fulton, Whitney, Morse, Cooper, and Edison.

Each life tells a young reader three things. It tells how a famous maker got his start. It tells what he built and what his work changed. Steamboats, the cotton gin, and the telegraph lead to electric light and sound. The book uses short, simple pages, with a fresh paragraph for nearly every sentence, shaped for children meeting invention as a set of human stories rather than a list of dates.
the-life-of-the-right-honourable-horatio: Mr. Harrison wrote his life of Horatio, Lord Viscount Nelson, in two volumes, and this record holds volume two, printed in London in 1806. Only the title page is present here. It carries Nelson full roll of honors as Baron Nelson of the Nile and Knight of the Bath. Duke of Bronte in Sicily and honorary grandee of Spain complete the list. A royal answer on the battle of Trafalgar stands as epigraph. The narrative of volume two itself is absent from this record.
the-pronunciation-of-english-words-deriv:
John Sargeaunt's Pronunciation of English Words Derived from the Latin appeared as S.P.E. Tract No. IV at the Clarendon Press in 1920. H. Bradley supplied a preface and notes. An introduction sketches how Latin was pronounced in England after Gregory's missionaries arrived. In careful speech it stayed close to first-century usage, the editor says, with six exceptions. Consonantal u sounded like modern v, and c before front vowels was pronounced ts.

G before front vowels resembled Latin consonantal i, and s between vowels matched the modern sound. The diphthongs ae and oe had simplified to a plain e. Ancient vowel quantities, the list continues, were also changing. A transcriber's note explains the bracketed symbols used for phonetic characters that plain text cannot show.
william-auvergne-de-universo:
William of Auvergne maps all things in De universo, his vast Latin work of near 1230. William was bishop of Paris and a sage of great range. His work takes in two great spans. One is the world of flesh, from stars to stones. One is the world of souls, with ranks of angels and swarms of demons.

He grants demons more room than most of his peers. Tales of marvels crowd his proofs. The work, in Latin, is a base text of the school lore on demons. Its scope is huge.
